name: CNN kernel / learned filter
short: A learned tensor of local filter weights.
body: A convolution layer learns weights shared across spatial positions. With multiple channels, each output filter combines neighborhoods from the relevant input channels.
example: An ordinary Conv2d with 3 input channels, 8 output channels and 3×3 filters has weights shaped 8×3×3×3: 216 numbers, plus optional biases.
note: PyTorch Conv2d implements cross-correlation. These weight tensors are distinct from the executable CPU or GPU kernels that apply them.

name: Convolution kernel
body: Convolution is the translation-invariant case of an integral operator: K(x,y)=k(x−y). A single function k describes how the signal is mixed at every location.
example: A normalized box kernel averages nearby values. An impulse convolved with k reproduces k.
note: Mathematical convolution reverses one operand relative to cross-correlation. Symmetric kernels hide this difference.

name: Discrete image / signal kernel
short: A small array of filter coefficients.
body: A finite collection of weights samples the neighborhood around each output location. Blur, sharpening, derivatives and edge detection use different weight patterns.
example: The centered filter [¼, ½, ¼] changes a neighborhood [2, 8, 2] into the weighted value 5.
note: Padding, origin, stride and whether the array is flipped affect the result. A filter need not be positive or normalized.

name: Integral-operator kernel
short: The two-variable function specifying an integral operator.
body: A function K(x,y) describes how an input value at y contributes to an output at x. The operator integrates those contributions. More generally, a Schwartz kernel can be a distribution rather than an ordinary function.
example: For K(x,y)=xy on [0,1] and f(y)=y, the output is x∫₀¹y²dy=x/3.
note: The function K and the nullspace ker(T) are both called kernels, even in the same discussion.

name: Density-estimation kernel
short: A normalized bump placed at each observation.
body: Kernel density estimation adds rescaled copies of a kernel around observed samples to estimate a density. Bandwidth sets the smoothing scale.
example: Place one Gaussian bump at each sample, then average the bumps. Smaller h reveals more detail and more sample noise.
note: A classical density kernel integrates to 1. It need not be a positive-semidefinite similarity kernel; higher-order estimation kernels can even have negative parts.

name: Heat / diffusion kernel
short: How a point concentration spreads over time.
body: For heat diffusion in ℝᵈ, the fundamental solution is a normalized Gaussian whose width grows with time. Convolving it with initial data solves the homogeneous heat equation.
example: In one dimension, the distribution represented by Hₜ has variance 2Dt. More elapsed time produces a wider, lower peak.
note: A heat kernel is a convolution kernel and, in suitable settings, a transition density. On a general manifold it is not a simple Gaussian of coordinate distance.

sources.title: The Fundamental Solution for the Heat Equation

name: Markov transition kernel
short: The distribution of the next state, given the current state.
body: A transition kernel specifies a Markov step. On a finite state space, it is a nonnegative row-stochastic matrix; on general spaces it is a probability kernel.
example: For P=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]], state 0 transitions to state 1 with probability 0.2. Every row sums to 1.
note: A Markov kernel need not be symmetric or positive semidefinite. An SVM kernel has different requirements.

name: Measure / probability kernel
short: A measurable assignment of a measure to each input.
body: A measure kernel assigns a measure K(x,·) to every x, measurably in x. A probability kernel assigns probability measures. Densities are optional, not part of the general definition.
example: K(x,B)=δₓ(B) describes deterministic copying of x: all probability is concentrated at x.
note: K(x,B) takes a measurable set as its second argument. A density k(x,y), when one exists, is a representation of this kernel.

sources.title: Transition kernels and completely positive maps

name: Morphological kernel
short: A neighborhood shape, also called a structuring element.
body: In morphology APIs, kernel often means a mask selecting the neighborhood for erosion, dilation, opening or closing. These operations need not be weighted sums.
example: For binary dilation, a cross-shaped neighborhood expands a set in its four cardinal directions.
note: A morphological kernel usually describes a shape or footprint. It is not generally a linear convolution filter.

name: Averaging / resolution kernel
short: How the true state appears in a retrieved state.
body: An averaging kernel differentiates the retrieval with respect to the true state. It describes sensitivity and smoothing in a recovered atmospheric profile or other inverse solution.
example: A retrieved value at one altitude may average the true state over nearby altitudes. An ideal noiseless, fully resolved retrieval has A=I.
note: Averaging kernels need not be simple positive averages. They differ from the forward measurement's sensitivity kernel.

sources.title: Intercomparison of remote sounding instruments
sources.publisher: C. D. Rodgers and B. J. Connor

name: Bethe–Salpeter interaction kernel
short: The interaction part of a two-particle integral equation.
body: The Bethe–Salpeter framework uses an interaction kernel to couple two-particle amplitudes. Approximations to it determine which interaction contributions the model includes.
example: A ladder approximation retains repeated exchanges built from an elementary exchange kernel.
note: This is a schematic operator equation; propagator factors, indices and integration conventions vary by formulation.

sources.title: Interaction kernel in the Bethe–Salpeter equation

name: Cauchy kernel
short: The reciprocal kernel in Cauchy's integral formula.
body: Cauchy's formula recovers a holomorphic function from its values on a surrounding contour by integrating against a reciprocal factor.
example: For f(ζ)=ζ² on a contour surrounding z, the integral returns z².
note: The contour orientation and the location of z matter. A Cauchy kernel is not the same object as a Cauchy probability density.

name: Collision / coagulation kernel
body: A coagulation kernel K(a,b) gives the rate at which particles of sizes a and b merge in a population-balance model. Collision kernels in kinetic equations likewise encode interaction rates.
example: The constant coagulation kernel assigns the same size-independent rate to every pair; additive and multiplicative kernels weight sizes differently.
note: Nonnegative interaction rates do not imply a positive-semidefinite ML kernel. Physical units are rate units, not similarity units.

name: Density / likelihood kernel
short: A density or likelihood with irrelevant constants removed.
body: In statistical calculations, kernel can mean the part of a density or likelihood left after factors constant in the variable of interest are dropped.
example: For a normal density with fixed variance, viewed as a function of μ, exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)) is its likelihood kernel.
note: Constant means constant in the variable being studied. If σ is unknown, the 1/σ factor cannot be discarded.

name: Dirichlet kernel
short: The convolution kernel for a Fourier partial sum.
body: Adding the frequency modes from −N through N produces a kernel that reconstructs the Nth Fourier partial sum.
example: D₁(θ)=1+2cosθ. Its oscillating lobes help explain why partial sums can overshoot near jumps.
note: It is not everywhere positive and is not a probability density. Its name does not make it the general kernel for a Dirichlet boundary problem.

sources.title: Fejér's Theorem and Convergence of Fourier Series

name: Dispersal kernel
short: A distribution of dispersal displacement or distance.
body: A dispersal kernel describes where seeds, spores or organisms arrive relative to their source. Its tails strongly affect long-range spread.
example: A narrow Gaussian models mostly local movement; a heavy-tailed distribution allows more rare long-distance arrivals.
note: A distance density and a density per unit area differ by a radial Jacobian. Always check the units and normalization.

sources.title: When will plant morphology affect the shape of a seed dispersal kernel?

name: Exchange–correlation kernel
short: A functional derivative of a potential with respect to density.
body: The exchange–correlation response kernel relates a small electron-density change to a change in the exchange–correlation potential.
example: An adiabatic local approximation yields a response local in time and space, represented using delta factors and a density-dependent derivative.
note: This is a response function in density-functional theory, not the core electrons of the historical atomic kernel.
